candidates.title: NTSB investigating fatal railcar accident in Oklahoma
candidates.excerpt: DURANT, Okla. — The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating after one person was killed during movement of railcars at a Durant business. The NTSB said on social media that the fatality occurred on an industry track at the plant for feed manufacturer Hardy Farms. Durant police said in a press release that the incident occurred Wednesday morning during the loading and movement of railcars not being moved by a locomotive, and that the person “was believed to have been ejected or become trapped beneath” a car that struck a derail device. Specialized heavy equipment was needed to reach the individual, who was pronounced dead at the scene. Video on the website of KXII-TV shows an overturned covered hopper on a business spur. Police said the identity of the person was not being released “out of respect for the individual and their family.” Durant and Union Pacific police are investigating, along with the Oklahoma Office of the Chief Medical Examiner. candidates.excerpt: China-India box rates double as import demand strains vessel space Vessel space demand from China to India continues to be strong, keeping container freight rates ... Historically high freight yields are driving a wave of dedicated container services between India and the Middle East, a tradelane that has been through a number of upheavals since the outbreak of Iran-US military tension. The latest example: Maersk has just rolled out a new container shuttle loop from India’s Nhava Sheva port (JNPA) to Khor Fakkan in the UAE, “to support customers seeking better service reliability”. The service, which began with the 2,600 teu Maersk Namibia departing JNPA on 24 September, is to initially offer a fortnightly frequency, according to industry sources. The standalone loop complements regular sailings by the Danish carrier between JNPA and Salalah in Oman, a key hub for the Gemini partners, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd. candidates.title: Why supply and demand no longer tell the whole story in container shipping
candidates.excerpt: Why supply and demand no longer tell the whole story in container shipping For much of container shipping’s history, market conditions could be understood through a relatively straightforward equation. When cargo demand grew faster than available vessel capacity, utilisation and freight rates generally rose. When capacity expanded more quickly than demand, rates typically came under pressure. That fundamental relationship has not changed. Supply and demand remain at the heart of container shipping, but the equation now contains more variables than it once did. Inventory decisions, geopolitical developments, sourcing shifts and constraints across ocean and inland networks can all influence how demand materialises and how much capacity is available in practice. As a result, understanding today’s market requires looking beyond cargo volumes and fleet size alone.
